Both my mom and stepdad have had widow maker heart attacks. My mom passed her one year since in November 2025, and then my dad had one in early January 2026. We were so incredibly lucky. My dad is a volunteer firefighter currently taking his EMT course, noticed the signs, and called 911 for my mom. 

When it came to him, he told her to call. He was sitting in the ER, hooked up to an EKG, and had the heart attack. They got him up to the cath lab and surgery started within 30 minutes. I'm so grateful for our local hospital. ❤
comments.author: @AnimeLove03

comments.text:
My grandma recently went for a scheduled oncology appointment where her doctor noticed her breathing sounded “off” and told her she needed to be sent to a cardiac unit immediately. Turns out had a severe blockage that could have turned into a widow-maker any day. She had a stent put in that day and says she feels 10x better. 
Weeks later, she went back to her oncologist and told him he saved her life and he teared up. I am so grateful to that doctor for giving me more time with my Grandma, my favorite person on the planet! I’m sure this patient’s family feels the same way.

comments.text:
At 19 years old I got really sick with what looked like a respiratory infection. I kept telling the doctors something was wrong and that I needed more imaging/care. They tried antibiotics, inhalers, breathing treatments, steroids and NOTHING worked. I deteriorated so bad I ended up crashing in the ER and it turned out I was in severe heart failure, BMP in the 20,000’s somewhere and an EF of 19. 
Same thing happened in 2024, but with an empyema. Urgent referral to ER for a CT scan and I was refused, a few days later I was back in the hospital for 16 days. They drained 2 liters off my right lung and I was on IV antibiotics the whole time. 
It is SO encouraging to see healthcare providers advocate for and help their own patients.
comments.author: @littlemissschweets

comments.text: At the ripe age of 44, I had a heart attack. As a woman, it never crossed my mind that it could be that. I brushed it off as a really bad case of acid reflux and took a few tums. A few hours later, I was up, in extreme pain,  vomiting and have diarrhea, and having problems breathing. As with this woman, I had a 95% blockage in my right coronary artery and they had to place two stents in order to get blood flowing correctly again. I would not wish this kind of pain on anyone. It just shows how different each attack is and how the body reacts to it. I'm am lucky to be here , just as Rachelle says. I can only say that you should advocate for your health. Be truthful with your doctor, but also make sure your doctor listens to you. Finding a good doctor is very hard. It took me 20 years to get a doctor that I felt listened to me.

comments.text:
Paramedic here. This is why I tell patients that there's nothing as a "small symptom". Yes, it could be a simple contact dermatitis or a mild sunburn, it can also be polymorphous light eruption, which although mostly benign, can be extremely annoying and it can be managed with some medications and high SPF sunscreen.
Never underestimate what you feel. If anything feels odd, go see a doctor; tell your doctor "hey doc, a couple of days ago I felt this and that". We're on the medical field, you can trust us with intimate information because the more we know about it, we can give a better care.

Thank you for speaking, Rachelle! And voicing how your experience was. And what answer you received when asking why you're the only woman in the room. I'm glad you received a good answer back there, too! And I hope it is a wake-up call for many!

As a woman who struggles with her health but atzends to it whenever my strength allows it (some of which with success, some still with a lit of question marks) I know how difficult it is to carry on especially when the answers are not this immediate and when you are left to do a lot of digging yourself.

It's not just about needing providers to be more aware and insurances enabling more time and resources for primary care doctors to be able to catch issues at all BEFORE they become debilitating! But it's also about our own agency as patient and about us asking questions when things are off and when doctors seem unsettled. To get a better grasp on urgency for ourselves. Because yes, we have a high load of burden but otger than maybe peer women and rare outstanding doctors, noone is going to push t our backs the way we push at the backs of everyone else, to get their health concerns sorted.

At the very least, we have to step up at pushing on our own backs, while society gets itself re-sorted.

comments.text: Not a heart attack but very similar. I had many struggles with energy and anemia for most of life. At around 15 I completely lost the ability to run because of how hard and fast my heartbeat felt. It was incredibly painful and I kept going to doctors because of this chest pain, i went as far as to measure my bpm as well (when standing it was over 160, when sitting 120, and when laying down 90) 6 months later the chest pain became so bad that I could barely walk my mom took me to a different GP who then referred me to an internist…that was my FIRST ekg, at the internist. Luckily my heart was fine but what we found via an ultrasound that the internist made me get aswell. We found an enormous and very active malignant paraganglioma, I had toxic chronic levels of nor-adrenaline. My blood pressure when emitted to the hospital was 160/140. Mind you each doctor visit tested my blood pressure but since I was a teenage girl instead of the doctors being shocked they simply did not believe it and thought it was machine errors. If this tumour was left in for maybe a month more I would have been dead. What shocks me the most is that it took 6 Months of constant doctor visits for my symptoms to have a doctor take the initiative to take an EKG. Im glad this was caught by you DrMike, even Obvious signs get ignored in women because sadly for women misdiagnosis is far too common

comments.text:
You story brought back memories...  Made me cry. Similar to mine. Mine just happened in 1 afternoon (in a few hours) my life was saved and changed forever.

My doctor didn't know, in fact I was in work when I got some chest pain, I asked my boss let me jump out to the pharmacy for some pain killers, and the pharmacist asked me what is it for?
And refused to give me "paracetamol" or any painkiller for this, based on my explanation, he rather I sent next door where was a "supposed to be" a walk-in doctor.

This doctor was only having a "few" (I guess rich) patient and didn't want take new patients, he told me go to a different walk-in doctor, so I left work the day (this was after about lunch time, I think the food had to do with it too) so I drove to a walk in doctor (that was near the hospital 3 minute walk)

The real walk-in doctor said it could be anything, muscle pain, stomach issue (acid reflex) or whatever but in case, just to be sure, he to the hospital for an ECG (he didn't have the equipment), so he sent me to the emergency unit... At the emergency, you still wait 5-10-15 hours 

So, I was waiting for my turn in the emergency waiting room with chest pain... maybe half an hour more, when the pain become so bad I almost collapsed and people around me (other patients, some other hospital workers, like these boys who help push patient around, and security) noticed my big pain, and they called for help. (These random people are my saviors)

Then someone came out and got me in a wheelchair, and soon got ECG, then blood, etc. Minutes later they were asking about what I took today, gave me some tablets, and a a bit of nitro-glycerine spray under my tongue, (and I guess aspirin...) .I have heart disease in my family members, so I knew what are these for... 

So it turned out, I had 3 blockages 99%, 70% and 50%, two days later they operated me (angioplasty) the 2 smaller one got fixed with stents (2 days later with angiography) and the third one 99-100%. Was not fixable, but they said the blood is still flowing into that area my heart created other ways, so I'll be ok. (what this mean exactly I don't know, was my heart muscled damaged badly or it's ok?) 

I was age 43 (now 49). My life was saved by the pharmacist and the 2nd walk-in doctor. Although, they all could've call ambulance instead of sending me around on my own in my own car.

Long story short definitely don’t ignore symptoms because its better to be safe than sorry, so glad she’s okay and thanks for sharing her story!

comments.text: As someone who’s mom and grandma (my other grandma before she passed was too, and a whole bunch of great relatives were at one point) are nurses, I’ve learned much more from Doctor Mike than either of them. They don’t talk about medical stuff almost at all, the most they’ve told me is “if you hurt, take a Tylenol or ibuprofen depending on the type of pain and what is causing it.” My mom, the director of nursing at a nursing home is the type of person to be like “if you’re not physically dying or bleeding out, you’re fine.” And I’ve gone through encephalitis when I was 10, she kept saying I was fine, it was just migraines, till I had a seizure. My grandma called 911, she never had a doubt that there was something going on, my mom finally realized it was a bit more than just a migraine. Still to this day, they rarely ever talk about medical stuff, even if I ask, I get “it’s hard to explain.” If it weren’t for Doctor Mike I would have never known the symptoms of a heart attack or literally anything major, aneurisms, strokes, etc. I don’t even remember what seizures are like (memory loss is part of encephalitis) my family won’t even talk about what happened, they just said I can’t ever drink alcohol. Great medical professionalism. 🥲 My mom never even gave me the period talk, I learned it through friends, YouTube and school. Her ‘talk’ was “there’s pads downstairs.” Her version of ‘the talk’ was “older guys will want something you’re not ready for, so be careful.” Even without being a nurse, parents should teach there kids simple things like puberty, sex-ed, symptoms of heart attacks, stroke, etc.

comments.text: My paternal grandfather died at 60 of a heart attack while shoveling snow. My dad died at 59.  My brother died at 49. Both my dad and brother had left ventricular free wall rupture. I am currently 51 and not a day goes by that I don’t think about dying. Every day I take inventory of how I feel overall. Any type of pain in my chest, abdomen or arm gives me an anxiety attack. One day out of the blue I felt like my heart was beating really hard. Not fast, but hard. My normal heart rate is in the 70s-80s. It was about 55. I was sweating all over (suddenly) and started throwing up over and over. I let it go for about 15min but then asked my son to drive me to the ER. They got me in and did an EKG and told me it was normal and sent me home. About 4mo later I was reading a different set of labs and came across my EKG which said possible septal infarct. Of course I looked it up and it said it could be because the leads weren’t placed exactly perfectly. So I asked to have it redone by my primary and it was fine. But I was upset that they originally told me it was normally knowing my history, and also put my chief complaint that day as nausea. I NEVER go to the ER. I wouldn’t go for nausea. I feel like they didn’t take me seriously. Then my primary ordered a treadmill and nuclear stress test which I did last June. No one ever called me with results or told me anything about it. My primary put in a cardiology consult at the same time as the stress test order (last May) and my appointment is next week. 11mo after my consult was placed. I just wish someone would understand what it feels like to wonder every day if you’re going to die and take my concerns seriously and please let me know what’s ACTUALLY going on with my heart. If it’s truly nothing then TELL ME THAT. Show me images. Talk to me.

I remember during my ER rotation, a patient was brought by his son complaining "my father has fever because he's sweating so much even under the AC!", they asked for just an antipyretic and wanted to leave. The father's vitals were normal; no fever, was stable and talking normally, but was covered in sweat. Did an ECG and it showed a massive heart attack, his only symptom wad diaphoresis.
Another patient once came just to ask for a refill medication of his GERD, but he was urgent and said the burning sensation is worse, he brushed it off as "I haven't taken my medication in a couple of days so it is expected", did an ECG and he was having a heart attack.
These 2 and other experiences taught me to always rule out MI in any patient with risk factors for it, even if the complaint was not even remotely related to the classic presentation.

I almost died 4 weeks ago, here’s that story- Spent 3 weeks in the hospital because on 1/14 my mom found me unresponsive, blue lips, foaming at the mouth, in respiratory distress, and I had just had my first ever seizure at the age of 31

She called 911 (ironically, my birthday is 9/11 😂), the paramedics stabilized me, got me in the ambulance, and I had two more seizures in the ambulance. I was in a vent for 6 days, and “woke up” on 1/19 in the hospital, not knowing what was happening, and I was experiencing ICU delusions/hallucination’s. I thought I didn’t have a face, I told the doctors/nurses I didn’t need glasses anymore because I took my eyes out, I thought the hospital staff were trying to unalive me/experiment on me, etc

I spent the next few days in the ICU being monitored, but didn’t know what was happening (because the delusions/hallucinations made me forget when the hospital staff told me what was happening), so I thought it I closed my eyes, I’d never open them again. So what did I do? I fought sleep/the meds they gave me, stared at the clock, and just sang Queens 🎶 keep yourself alive, keep yourself alive, all you got to do is keep yourself alive 🎶 on repeat for DAYS 

Finally, I was moved to recovery, started becoming more lucid, however….. I still didn’t fully understand what was happening, and thought either I had been committed because I went mad, or, my mom went mad, and was trying to get my commitment due to munchhausen by proxy

I’ve broken up dog fights completely alone, been mauled on the face by a dog, resulting in needing reconstructive surgery to my eyelids/tear duct, and needing stents in the tear duct to keep them open for 3 months, and I can tell you WITH 👏🏻 OUT 👏🏻 A 👏🏻 DOUBT 👏🏻 this was the scariest thing I’ve ever experienced!!
